records.title: Sell from Stock
records.memory_hook: Own stock → confirm → deliver → PGI → invoice.
records.lead_summary: The standard branch is useful because every special process changes one of its controls. A normal stock item is typically determined as TAN; its schedule line then controls ATP, requirements transfer and delivery. The key diagnostic path is item category → schedule line → plant/shipping point → stock → PGI → billing.

trace.control: Standard sales order
trace.effect: Creates the normal external customer sales contract and supplies document-pricing control.

trace.control: Standard item; documented standard example TAN
determined_by: item category group such as NORM
trace.effect: Enables standard pricing, schedule lines, delivery and billing behavior.

trace.control: Documented standard schedule-line example CP
trace.effect: Transfers requirements, performs availability check and is delivery relevant.

trace.control: Own plant stock
trace.effect: No customer- or order-specific special stock is required for the baseline.

trace.control: Goods issue; documented API example movement type 601
trace.effect: Reduces own stock and creates the cost-side logistics/accounting event.

trace.control: Delivery-related customer billing plus condition-technique pricing
trace.effect: Creates the customer receivable and revenue-side commercial result.

trace.control: SD → Delivery Management/MM-IM → FI/CO
trace.effect: Stock, COGS, revenue, tax and receivables become linked to the sales flow.

data_hinges.if_wrong: A standard item can become a non-standard item or fail item-category determination.
Schedule-line determination, ATP or requirements transfer can change.
ATP, shipping point, stock source and company-code context can change.
Shipping point may be missing or different.
Correct condition records can still be invisible because the wrong procedure was selected.

failures.symptom: Order exists but cannot be delivered.
failures.trace: Check item category delivery relevance → schedule line delivery relevance → confirmed quantity → shipping point → delivery block/incompletion.

failures.symptom: Unexpected zero or late confirmation.
failures.trace: Check plant and material → MRP type → schedule line → ATP scope/checking rule → stock/receipts.

failures.symptom: Missing or wrong price.
failures.trace: Prove pricing procedure first, then access sequence and condition record.

tests.setup: Create one normal stock order item with known stock and complete master data.
Use a plant/shipping combination with missing shipping-point determination.
assert: order becomes incomplete for shipping rather than failing later without explanation

records.title: Third-Party Order Processing
records.memory_hook: We sell it; the supplier ships it.
records.lead_summary: The decisive change is that SAP replaces your own delivery chain with an account-assigned procurement chain. In the documented standard example TAS + CS creates a purchase requisition; the supplier sends goods directly to the customer. Billing can be controlled by supplier invoice receipt quantity, so MM-IV becomes part of the sales billing dependency.

trace.control: Customer sales order remains the commercial anchor
trace.effect: Customer pricing and receivable still belong to SD even though physical supply moves to Purchasing.

trace.control: Documented standard third-party item category TAS
determined_by: third-party-relevant item category group such as BANS or manual allowed category
trace.effect: The sales item is not fulfilled from your own outbound stock.

trace.control: Documented standard schedule line CS
trace.effect: Creates a purchase requisition; documented standard settings use PO type NB, purchasing item category S and account assignment X.

trace.control: No normal own stock receipt required
trace.effect: Supplier ships directly to customer; a statistical goods receipt may be posted but is not mandatory for the basic process.

trace.control: Supplier delivery is outside your outbound delivery
trace.effect: Delivery dates/quantities must be synchronized through purchasing confirmations rather than your warehouse execution.

trace.control: Order-related billing; standard TAS can use billing relevance F
determined_by: supplier invoice receipt quantity or configured alternative
trace.effect: Customer billing may wait for supplier invoice verification and use the invoiced supplier quantity as the billing basis.

trace.control: SD → MM-PUR → supplier → MM-IV → SD Billing
trace.effect: A sales problem can originate in Purchasing or Invoice Verification even when the customer order looks correct.

data_hinges.if_wrong: No third-party procurement trigger or wrong fulfillment branch.
Purchase requisition is not created or has wrong procurement control.
Sales confirmation dates can be stale or unrealistic.
Billing due list can remain empty when invoice-receipt-based billing is used.

failures.symptom: Sales order saved, but no purchase requisition.
failures.trace: Check TAS determination → CS schedule line → PR creation control → incompletion/errors.

failures.symptom: Supplier delivered, but customer invoice is not due.
failures.trace: Check TAS billing relevance/copy control → supplier invoice receipt → invoice quantity → billing status.

failures.symptom: Customer confirmation and PO confirmation disagree.
failures.trace: Check confirmation control key and whether PO acknowledgment has updated the sales schedule lines.

tests.setup: Create a third-party sales item with supplier and purchasing data.
Complete supplier delivery but omit invoice receipt in an invoice-receipt-based billing setup.
assert: customer billing remains blocked/not due for the expected reason

records.title: Purchase-to-Order / Individual Purchase Order
records.memory_hook: Buy for this customer, receive it into our custody, then deliver it.
records.lead_summary: PTO looks similar to TPO only until you ask where the goods physically arrive. The supplier ships to us, not directly to the customer. The purchased quantity is pegged to the sales order item and is managed as sales order stock, so the same supply cannot silently satisfy another demand.

trace.control: Customer sales order
trace.effect: Creates the customer demand that owns the procurement segment.

trace.control: Individual-purchase-order item behavior
determined_by: item category determination or allowed manual alternative
trace.effect: The item creates an order-specific procurement requirement.

trace.control: Order-specific purchase requisition assigned to the sales order item
trace.effect: PR/PO cannot satisfy unrelated customer requirements.

trace.control: Sales order stock; special stock indicator E in the classic model
trace.effect: Received goods are segregated for the sales order item.

trace.control: Supplier → our goods receipt → our outbound delivery
determined_by: goods receipt into sales order stock
trace.effect: Unlike TPO, our warehouse/logistics execution remains in the chain.

trace.control: Delivery-related customer billing
trace.effect: Customer billing is tied to our delivery rather than supplier invoice receipt.

trace.control: SD → MM-PUR → MM-IM sales-order stock → Delivery → FI/CO
trace.effect: Procurement cost and customer revenue can be tracked to the same sales-order context.

data_hinges.if_wrong: Supply may no longer be protected for the customer order.
Customer confirmation date drifts because purchasing scheduling drives material availability.
The sales order can remain undeliverable although the PO exists.

failures.symptom: Purchased goods are visible, but not available to the intended sales order.
failures.trace: Check PO account assignment → special stock E / sales-order reference → GR posting destination.

failures.symptom: PO and GR complete, but delivery cannot be created.
failures.trace: Check sales-order stock assignment → item/schedule-line delivery relevance → stock/ATP → delivery block.

failures.symptom: Confirmed date is later than expected.
failures.trace: Check purchasing processing time → planned delivery time → GR processing time → factory calendar.

tests.setup: Create an order-specific procurement item and complete PR/PO/GR.
assert: unrelated order cannot consume the stock

tests.setup: Create a second customer order for the same material.
assert: first order's sales-order stock is not used for the second demand

records.title: Customer Consignment
records.lead_summary: Consignment is easiest to own when you separate four events: fill-up, issue, return, pickup. Fill-up moves your inventory to customer special stock without customer billing. Issue consumes that special stock and becomes billable. Return reverses an issued quantity back into consignment stock; pickup brings unsold consignment stock back to plant stock.

trace.control: Consignment sub-process: fill-up / issue / return / pickup
trace.effect: The same physical material follows different ownership and billing rules depending on the sub-process.

trace.control: Consignment-specific item behavior
trace.effect: Controls whether the step is billing relevant and from/to which stock segment it acts.

trace.control: Delivery/returns schedule appropriate to the consignment event
trace.effect: Creates outbound or return logistics without confusing ownership transfer.

trace.control: Customer consignment special stock W
trace.effect: Stock can be physically at the customer while remaining company-owned.

trace.control: Fill-up uses a stock-transfer goods movement; documented movement catalog includes 631 for customer-consignment transfer and 633 for issue
trace.effect: Fill-up increases customer special stock; issue reduces it and total company stock.

trace.control: Fill-up and pickup are not customer billing events; issue is invoiced; return can create credit
determined_by: consignment sub-process and item billing relevance
trace.effect: Physical movement and commercial ownership transfer are intentionally decoupled.

trace.control: SD → Delivery/MM-IM special stock → Billing/FI when ownership changes
trace.effect: Inventory and revenue timing follow different events.

data_hinges.if_wrong: Stock can be posted under the wrong consignee and become operationally invisible.
The system can move stock correctly but produce the wrong billing consequence.
Users may mistake customer-located stock for unrestricted plant stock.

failures.symptom: Consignment stock exists but not for the expected customer.
failures.trace: Check special-stock partner/customer assignment on order and material document.

failures.symptom: Customer appears billable on fill-up.
failures.trace: Check document/item category and billing relevance; fill-up should represent stock relocation, not ownership transfer.

failures.symptom: Consignment issue cannot post.
failures.trace: Check customer special stock quantity → plant → batch/stock segment → issue order quantity.

tests.setup: Run fill-up, partial issue, return and pickup for one customer.
assert: fill-up moves value into customer special stock without customer invoice
issue reduces consignment stock and creates billing relevance
return restores consignment stock and supports credit
pickup restores plant stock without customer revenue

records.title: Classic Intercompany Sales
records.memory_hook: One company sells; another company delivers; internal billing bridges them.
records.lead_summary: Classic intercompany is a legal-entity split around one external customer order. The delivering plant belongs to another company code. External customer billing remains with the selling company, while intercompany billing transfers value from delivering to selling company. The Lead question is not only 'is the plant different?' but whether the required internal customer, pricing and billing relationships exist.

trace.control: Selling sales area owns the external customer order
trace.effect: Defines which company owns the customer contract and external receivable.

trace.control: Intercompany-relevant item because delivering plant belongs to another company code
trace.effect: Adds an internal commercial relationship without changing the external customer.

trace.control: Delivering company plant supplies the customer
trace.effect: Physical fulfillment occurs in another legal entity.

trace.control: Stock belongs to delivering company until its logistics posting
trace.effect: Inventory and COGS originate in the delivering company.

trace.control: Outbound delivery/PGI from delivering plant
trace.effect: Triggers physical stock reduction in delivering company.

trace.control: External customer invoice plus intercompany billing; documented standard intercompany billing type IV and conditions PI01/PI02
trace.effect: Selling company bills customer; delivering company bills selling company internally.

trace.control: SD/LE across company codes → FI-AR/AP and internal margin
trace.effect: Two legal entities recognize different revenue/cost relationships from one customer demand.

data_hinges.if_wrong: Process can fall back to normal domestic fulfillment or use the wrong legal entity.
Intercompany invoice cannot be created/posted correctly.
Internal transfer price is missing even when customer pricing is correct.

failures.symptom: Customer invoice exists, intercompany invoice does not.
failures.trace: Check intercompany billing relevance/type IV assignment → internal customer → delivery/billing status.

failures.symptom: Intercompany invoice has missing/incorrect internal price.
failures.trace: Check PI01/PI02 condition records and internal pricing configuration, not customer PR00 first.

failures.symptom: Delivery comes from an unexpected legal entity.
failures.trace: Check plant determination and plant↔company-code/sales-area assignments.

tests.setup: Create order in selling company with delivering plant in another company code.
assert: external order belongs to selling company
delivery is executed by delivering plant
customer invoice posts in selling company
intercompany invoice posts between legal entities
internal pricing is independent from customer pricing

records.title: Advanced Intercompany Sales
records.memory_hook: The legal-entity split becomes an orchestrated document chain.
records.lead_summary: AIC keeps the external standard sales order as the leading document but makes the internal leg explicit. A different-company-code delivering plant triggers an intercompany PO and an intercompany sales order when the scenario is enabled and quantity is confirmed. Valuated stock in transit and transfer-of-control events separate physical departure from legal/economic control.

trace.control: Leading external standard sales order
trace.effect: Owns the customer promise and starts value-chain orchestration.

trace.control: AIC relevance when delivering plant company code differs from sales-area company code and AIC is enabled
trace.effect: Marks the item for generated intercompany procurement and sales documents.

trace.control: Automatic intercompany PO in selling company; intercompany sales order in delivering company
trace.effect: One generated PO per delivering plant; internal demand becomes explicit and monitorable.

trace.control: Transit plant and valuated stock in transit
trace.effect: Inventory can remain valuated while goods move between legal control points.

trace.control: Documented AIC sales-item movement type 687 into VSiT
trace.effect: Physical PGI does not necessarily equal final external transfer of control.

trace.control: Customer invoice plus intercompany customer invoice and supplier invoice verification
trace.effect: External and internal invoices are separate process steps; financial synchronization extends into MM-IV.

trace.control: SD → MM-PUR → generated intercompany SD → Delivery/VSiT → SD Billing → MM-IV → FI/CO + Value Chain Monitoring
trace.effect: Failures are cross-module and should be diagnosed through the generated document chain, not transaction by transaction.

data_hinges.if_wrong: AIC relevance and generated PO ownership can change.
Unconfirmed item is not transferred to the intercompany PO.
Financial valuation/profitability context for VSiT is wrong or incomplete.
VSiT postings and accounting timing can be wrong even if physical delivery is correct.

failures.symptom: External order is AIC-intended but no intercompany PO appears.
failures.trace: Check different company codes → AIC enablement → confirmed quantity → purchasing org/group defaults → value-chain messages.

failures.symptom: Some generated documents exist but chain stops.
failures.trace: Use Monitor Value Chains → identify failed step → verify predecessor document/status instead of recreating documents manually.

failures.symptom: Inventory/accounting timing disagrees with physical movement.
failures.trace: Check transit plant → movement 687/value-chain mapping → internal/external transfer-of-control dates → Incoterms.

tests.setup: Create confirmed external order with delivering plant in another company code and valid AIC setup.
assert: customer and internal billing steps exist

tests.setup: Create AIC-relevant item with zero confirmed quantity.
assert: item is not transferred to intercompany PO until confirmation exists

records.title: Make-to-Order
records.memory_hook: The sales order creates its own supply segment.
records.lead_summary: MTO is where an SD-only explanation stops being useful. Standard item/schedule-line keys can still look ordinary, while the requirement type and planning strategy make the supply order-specific. Strategy group/MRP group determine requirement behavior; production or procurement then creates sales-order stock that only the owning order can consume.

trace.control: Customer sales order is the demand and cost/revenue reference
trace.effect: The sales item becomes the anchor for order-specific supply and, depending on design, cost/revenue collection.

trace.control: Documented strategy-20 example still uses item category TAN for NORM
trace.effect: MTO behavior does not require inventing a special SD item category in the modern requirements-type model.

trace.control: Documented strategy-20 example uses schedule line CP; requirement type KE is found from strategy group 20
determined_by: item category + MRP type for schedule line
strategy group/MRP group for requirements type
trace.effect: Sales demand drives order-specific production/planning rather than generic make-to-stock consumption.

trace.control: Sales order stock
determined_by: requirements class/type and MTO valuation design
trace.effect: Finished goods/components can be segregated for the owning sales order; stock can be valuated or non-valuated depending on design.

trace.control: Production receipts into order-specific stock, then outbound delivery/PGI
trace.effect: PP execution feeds the exact customer demand rather than unrestricted inventory.

trace.control: Customer sales pricing plus delivery/order billing according to scenario; cost/revenue can be collected on the sales order item
trace.effect: Margin analysis depends on both SD revenue and order-specific production/procurement cost flow.

trace.control: SD → MRP/PP (or procurement) → sales-order stock → Delivery → CO/FI
trace.effect: A sales-order confirmation problem may actually be a PP strategy or MRP master-data problem.

data_hinges.if_wrong: Requirement type and MTO planning behavior change.
Fallback requirements-type determination can differ.
MTO planning and costing context is incomplete or wrong.
FI/CO timing and inventory valuation behavior differ materially.

failures.symptom: Sales order exists but planning does not create order-specific supply.
failures.trace: Check strategy group/MRP group → requirement type → requirements class → plant/MRP run → procurement type.

failures.symptom: Finished product goes to unrestricted stock instead of sales-order stock.
failures.trace: Check requirement type/class and account assignment/settlement design before changing delivery settings.

failures.symptom: Order confirms against the wrong supply logic.
failures.trace: Check MTO ATP checking rule/scope and order-specific receipts rather than only unrestricted stock.

tests.setup: Use a material with strategy group 20 and valid plant/MRP settings.
assert: requirement type KE in documented strategy-20 example
receipt belongs to sales order stock

tests.setup: Change strategy group to a make-to-stock strategy in a controlled test material.
assert: requirements behavior changes even if SD item category remains TAN, proving that MTO control sits deeper than item-category memory
